candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: Hypotheses should be evaluated by combining their prior probabilities with evidence that is likelier given their truth than their falsity.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted affirmative opening explicitly identifies Matthew as the speaker and presents his stated epistemological method.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This Bayesian framework supplies the inferential standard used throughout the affirmative case to compare theism with atheism.
candidates.contextSummary: After introductory remarks, Matthew establishes a prior-and-likelihood approach and illustrates it with poker, dark matter, and historical inference.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: Theism has a reasonable prior probability because one unlimited fundamental mind is simple, non-arbitrary, omnipotent, omniscient, and morally perfect.
candidates.attributionBasis: The affirmative speaker explicitly announces the application of his methodology to God and develops the simplicity argument continuously.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move answers the prior-probability component of the affirmative Bayesian case and defines the perfect being whose existence is defended.
candidates.contextSummary: Matthew invokes simplicity and non-arbitrariness, argues that minds are irreducibly fundamental, and characterizes God as an unlimited instance of mind.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: The life-permitting fine-tuning of physical constants is much more probable under theism than atheism and therefore supports God's existence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matthew labels fine-tuning as his first evidential line and explicitly compares its likelihood under God and atheism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Fine-tuning is one of the affirmative opening's enumerated primary evidential arguments for the debate's perfect-being proposition.
candidates.contextSummary: The affirmative describes narrow life-permitting constant ranges, emphasizes their alleged chance improbability, and says a good God would select values permitting life.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: Consciousness and the universe's stable, complexity-producing laws are more expected if a good God exists than in a godless material reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: The affirmative opening clearly marks these as its second and third lines of evidence and develops both without a speaker change.
candidates.loadBearingReason: These two linked likelihood arguments provide independent major evidential supports for the affirmative cumulative case beyond physical fine-tuning.
candidates.contextSummary: Matthew argues that subjectivity needs special laws under atheism and that random laws usually yield chaos or trivial patterns rather than valuable complex structure.

candidates.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
candidates.proposition: An individual's existence favors the maximum possible population, which is allegedly much likelier under a limitless good God than under atheism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matthew introduces the fact that the listener exists as his fourth evidential line and gives an extended first-person exposition of it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The anthropic argument occupies a substantial portion of the affirmative opening and is presented as a distinct, powerful evidential route to theism.
candidates.contextSummary: Using coin, card, birth-rank, and competing-infinity examples, Matthew argues that existence becomes likelier with more people and ultimately supports a divine multiverse.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Rational confidence should track the strength, testability, and empirical support of evidence, with judgment reserved when strong support is absent.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the floor to Matt, whose uninterrupted negative opening explicitly frames and explains his evidential standard.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This evidential-warrant standard establishes the negative side's governing burden and directly structures its rejection of belief in the proposed being.
candidates.contextSummary: Matt distinguishes mere consistency from strong support, discusses varying confidence and imperfect quantification, and concludes that belief requires sufficient rational warrant.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Humans lack a reliable means to distinguish extreme power, knowledge, and goodness from genuine omnipotence, omniscience, and moral perfection.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly turns to each property in the motion and continuously develops the epistemic limits of identifying those properties.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly contests whether evidence could warrant belief in the specific all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being named by the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew's characterization of an unlimited mind as omnipotent, omniscient, and morally perfect.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt argues that sufficiently advanced beings could appear divine without being maximal and that ordinary evidence cannot establish perfection rather than merely extraordinary ability.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Divine hiddenness, unreliable religious predictions, and preventable conflict over God's existence count against an omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect being.
candidates.attributionBasis: The negative speaker develops a continuous objection from God's nonappearance, unfalsifiable intervention claims, and morally troubling hiddenness.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly challenges both the existence and moral perfection of the precise being in the motion using observable features of the world.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew's claim that the world's valuable features are expected under a limitless and morally perfect God.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt contrasts dependable natural models with elastic God claims and argues that a perfect being would not remain hidden while people fight over its existence.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Greater likelihood under intentional design does not establish that design actually occurred, so probabilistic comparisons alone cannot justify inferring God.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt introduces alleged errors about causality and probability, then supplies an extended dice example that continues into the locked lookahead.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection targets the affirmative case's recurring inference from observations being more probable under God to warranted belief that God exists.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matthew's repeated Bayesian inference that evidence likelier under theism than atheism warrants belief in God.

candidates.contextSummary: Matt contrasts rolled double sixes with deliberately placed dice and argues that comparative likelihood from one observation cannot determine intentional causation.
